results.title: Model Artifacts | AI Glossary by Posium
results.content: # Model Artifacts. Model artifacts are the tangible outputs produced during the lifecycle of a machine learning model, including the trained model, metadata, and associated files necessary for deployment and reproducibility. Model artifacts represent the culmination of the machine learning model development process. They are the essential components required to deploy, serve, and manage a trained model in a production environment. These artifacts go beyond just the serialized model file itself and encompass all the supporting data and information needed to ensure the model functions correctly and can be reliably reproduced. **What Constitutes a Model Artifact?**. A comprehensive set of model artifacts typically includes the following:. * **The Trained Model:** This is the core artifact, representing the learned parameters and structure of the machine learning model. + **License Information:** Specifies the licensing terms for the model. * **Preprocessing Code:** Machine learning models often require input data to be preprocessed before it can be fed into the model. The code used for preprocessing should be included as an artifact to ensure consistent data transformation during both training and inference. * **Environment Configuration:** This artifact specifies the software dependencies and hardware requirements needed to run the model. The proper management and versioning of model artifacts are crucial for several reasons:. * **Reproducibility:** Artifacts enable the reproduction of the model's training process and results. * **Deployment:** Artifacts provide all the necessary components for deploying the model to a production environment. * **Monitoring and Auditing:** Metadata within the artifacts allows for tracking model performance over time and identifying potential issues. * **Governance and Compliance:** In regulated industries, model artifacts are essential for demonstrating compliance with regulatory requirements. Effective model artifact management is a key aspect of MLOps (Machine Learning Operations). Tools and platforms are available to help manage the lifecycle of model artifacts, including versioning, storage, and deployment. These tools often integrate with other MLOps components, such as data pipelines, model training platforms, and monitoring systems. In summary, model artifacts are more than just the trained model file. They represent a comprehensive package of all the necessary components for deploying, serving, and managing a machine learning model in a reliable and reproducible manner.

results.title: Detection, Evasion, and the Pursuit of Immutable Artifacts - CardinalOps
results.content: After years of drowning in telemetry, chasing ghost alerts, and fine-tuning SIEM rules, I’ve come to believe detection isn’t about more data — it’s about intentional signal design. In this post I’ll share some reflections on my journey, as I shift my focus on quality, not quantity, to build rules with less noise, more context, and a sharper focus on what really matters in detection: immutable artifacts. In detection engineering, immutable artifacts are the golden signals—the unchangeable traces an attacker leaves behind, no matter what tool, technique, or obfuscation they use. But we should aspire to write detections that find immutable artifacts that the attacker is going to leave behind 100% of the time, and that are not subject to obfuscation, source code modifications, or anything that the attacker controls. Shifting your focus to immutable artifacts anchors your detections on behaviors that must occur regardless of the tool or method.

results.title: DataDreamer: A Tool for Synthetic Data Generation and Reproducible LLM Workflows
results.content:
Title: DataDreamer: A Tool for Synthetic Data Generation and Reproducible LLM Workflows
# DataDreamer: A Tool for Synthetic Data Generation and Reproducible LLM Workflows. Today, many researchers use LLMs in synthetic data generation, task evaluation, fine-tuning, distillation, and other model-in-the-loop research workflows. DataDreamer helps researchers implement state-of-the-art emerging workflows involving LLMs such as synthetic data generation, fine-tuning, instruction-tuning, and alignment. DataDreamer helps researchers implement workflows while crucially producing output that is compatible with open science and reproducible ideals with minimal effort, through automatic caching, reproducibility fingerprints, and more best-practice artifacts. These workflows can be uniquely complex to both implement and reproduce due to requiring multiple rounds that chain together synthetic data generation, automatic evaluation, and model re-training. Synthetic data and model cards are automatically produced by recursively tracing through all steps, models, and trainers that DataDreamer used to produce the dataset or model. DataDreamer collects this information and produces a synthetic data card (or model card) that reports the information along with reproducibility information for each step, model, and trainer in the workflow. Since DataDreamer handles this distributed orchestration automatically, users can build multi-stage workflows involving data generation, data processing, and training on multiple GPUs all in a single Python program, obviating the use of orchestration through multiple shell scripts. While experimental workflows can often be sensitive to model choice and the transferability of prompts can be unreliable (Liu et al., 2023), for reproducibility purposes and for ease of experimentation, workflow implementation code should attempt to minimize dependence on a specific model and should allow other researchers to easily substitute one LLM for another. DataDreamer makes this simple by automatically saving the results of each step in a multi-stage workflow in an easily inspectable Hugging Face datasets format (Lhoest et al., 2021). We introduce DataDreamer, an open source Python package for implementing common patterns and workflows involving LLMs. We believe DataDreamer provides both practical and scientific utility to the research community and that its adoption can help advance the rate of research progress in workflows involving LLMs by making implementation easier and making research output reproducible and extendable. We believe the broader impacts of this work to be largely positive, making state-of-the-art LLM workflows both easier and more accessible to implement and reproduce as well as reducing carbon emissions through DataDreamer’s caching system that helps researchers avoid expensive re-computation when possible.

results.content: * **2024 March 28:** cTuning, MLCommons and cKnowledge has released a new version of the Collective Mind automation framework with a collection of reusable and technology-agnostic recipes to make it easier to compose and benchmark AI systems across rapidly evolving and commodity models, data set, software and hardware: see how CM helped to automate MLPerf inference v4.0 submissions and check a presentation at MLPerf-Bench workshop @ HPCA'24 of a new project to compose high-performance and cost-effective AI systems. Since criteria for the ACM "Artifacts Evaluated – Reusable" badge are quite vague, we partnered with the MLCommons task force on automation and reproducibility to add their unified interface (MLCommons CM) to the submitted artifacts to make them more portable, reproducible and reusable. That is why we decided to set up the Artifact Evaluation process at conferences to help the community validate results from accepted papers with the help of independent evaluators while collaborating with ACM and IEEE on a common methodology, reproducibility checklist and tools to automate this tedious process.

results.title: From Principles to Practice: Curating Research Artifacts for Reproducibility - ADS
results.content:
Title: From Principles to Practice: Curating Research Artifacts for Reproducibility - ADS
## ADS. ## From Principles to Practice: Curating Research Artifacts for Reproducibility. #### Abstract. Empirical claims reported in scientific journals typically rest upon data, software, code, documentation, and other digital artifacts which together make up a research compendium (Gentleman & Lang, 2004). The ability to reproduce scientific findings based on computational methods and reported by the original author is imperative (NASEM, 2019): It is meant to reveal the procedures described by the original author and to verify the findings reported in the scientific publication. To enable reproducibility over time requires proper stewardship of the compendium. A key principle guiding the curation and stewardship of the research compendium is the ability to reuse it and its component artifacts without the need to refer to the original author (King, 1995, Peer et al., 2014). The idea is echoed in the concept of intelligent openness (Royal Society, 2012) and in the OAIS model, whereby digital objects need to be independently understandable to (and usable by) the Designated Community... without needing the assistance of the experts who produced the information (CCSDS, 2012). In this presentation we will discuss what it means to care for these artifacts so as to increase their reusability and facilitate reproducibility in the long term. We will describe how curating for reproducibility (CURE) operationalizes these principles. We will also a describe how CURE practices relate to recommended practices for the curation of data, code, and software more generally and how these practices relate to FAIR, as well as other standards and guidelines. References: Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems. Reference model for an Open Archival Information System (OAIS) (Magenta Book CCSDS 650.0-M-2). Statistical analyses and reproducible research. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Reproducibility and replicability in science. Peer, L., Green, A., & Stephenson, E. Committing to data quality review. International Journal of Digital Curation, 9(1). The Royal Society (2012), Science as an open enterprise. Science Policy Centre, London, Royal Society. ### No Sources Found.
